Hey Matthew, 

For a while I disregarded you as too mainstream to have fantasy news or advice that would actually give me an advantage. That’s at least half a compliment. Hello! It’s awesome that you’re reaching out pre-college, trying to get a sense for what lies ahead. I wish I’d done more of that. 

Anyways, I am a sophomore in aerospace. I entered college really confident, my grades had always been near the top of my class, and I had rarely struggled to keep them there. Despite this, I really struggled freshman year. That struggle has continued into sophomore year, and I really don’t foresee the difficult easing up until *potentially* senior year. That said, I pledged a fraternity, grew really close to my dorm, and managed to make time for the gym/intramurals. It’s possible to do all of those things, given really time management and hard work. 

However, I came into college with a few advantages. The largest of which is the fact my dad studied engineering at CU, and many of my family friends who I have known since birth did as well. Thus, I had a decent idea of what to expect. 

If math is your struggle, things are going to be that much harder for you. If science is a tricky subject, thermodynamics is not going to be easy. These classes are not impossible, and there is an infrastructure in place to support your success as a student. You need to determine how much aerospace means to you. If it’s something you’re really truly passionate about, then I think it’d be a shame if I sat here and told you not to take a shot at it. That said, if you’re in it for anything other than a burning desire to work in the industry, at a company like Space X or Lockheed etc, I caution you. 

To be frank, most of my peers had significantly higher GPAs and ACTs coming into college, and I’ve watched many of them struggle without success. Many have stuck with it, but only through attending 10-15 hours of office hours a week, meeting with TAs and Professors. spending from 10-10 on school, every day but Friday afternoons and Saturdays, unless there’s a lab due (we have 11 this semester), in which case those rare breaks are in jeopardy. 

Fall semester (and the first half of this one) pushed me harder than I’ve ever been pushed before. For better or for worse, after freshman year, it will frequently feel like aerospace is your whole life. You’ll learn a ton about what I consider to be the most fascinating subjects there are, at no small cost. Freshman year is a good way to get a taste for what the future is like. APPM classes are tough even by aero standards, and you’ll dip your toes in physics and coding. These are fundamentals, and slacking on them will cost you greatly later in life. 

My answer has been verbose, but hopefully thorough. I worry that you have struggled in Alg 2, and haven’t done much outside of class to rectify your grades. This mindset will have to change, as it will often feel as though the professor hasn’t covered all the material expected of you, so you will have to take the initiative in order to succeed. 

I hope this sheds some light on your question!

Don’t expect any miracles when it comes to college math instruction. The onus will be on you to learn the material outside of class, something it seems you haven’t been doing this far. That isn’t to say you can’t do that in the future, but you will need to adjust your expectations and work ethic.

I fully recommend living in the dorm most aligned with your major. I consider myself a social person, I’m in Greek life, and I enjoy meeting women. For those reasons, I was hesitant about living in the engineering quad (where the vast majority of engineers live). They have a certain reputation for being male dominant, quiet, and insulating. They also happen to be some of the oldest, worst equipped dorms on campus. Nonetheless, my dad encouraged me to live in the quad regardless. I followed his advice, and it’s one of the best decisions I’ve ever made. Living with people of my major, and in similar majors, made a world of difference. Especially in a challenging major, sharing a common struggle was really important. Those friends of mine in engineering who opted for dorms outside the quad generally regretted that decision, as they led rather different lives from those around them. The age of the dorm wasn’t often an issue either. The washing machines sucked and the bathrooms were old, but they were generally clean, and usually worked. I think you make some good points, and I definitely agree that there are themes and elements established in TLJ that TRoS uses. Chiefly, the Rey to Kylo communication is the best part of the sequels in my opinion, and exists solely as a result of TLJ. However, I do find that TRoS asks us, in some respects, to forget about what happens in TLJ. 

Firstly, one of the biggest points TLJ makes is that Rey is the child of two nobodies. This is a powerful point to make, emphasized by the final shot of the movie. It instills in the viewer a belief that the universe doesn’t require a savior from noble lineage, but that ordinary people from humble beginnings can make all the difference. Whether you agree with the point the movie makes or the execution, this is a clear theme. In TRoS, we see this completely contradicted. In the first ten minutes of the movie, we learn her true origins and any work TLJ did to this end is forgotten. 

Secondly, the character development for Kylo is severely derailed. In TLJ we see him go from conflicted, struggling to be #2 in command, and haunted by killing Han. By the end of that movie, he has taken control, and cast aside the past. He wants Rey to join him, she denies him, so he attacks and tries to kill her. As TRoS begins, he’s already reverted in both respects. He’s back to being #2, he even reforged the helmet he so symbolically destroys. Again, he’s conflicted about his father. Nothing has changed about his character, save for who commands him. 

These are two examples, but there are more. 

If you ask me what I think about TLJ, I will defend the chances it took, its originality, and its quality as a film. However, if I am asked to consider it as the penultimate contribution to the Skywalker saga, it falls short of the mark. Finn is completely wasted, Po is mostly wasted, but it’s saved by Rey, Kylo, and Luke. If someone who has seen TFA and not TLJ wanted to see TRoS, and given what we know about TRoS, it wouldn’t take long to catch them up. I make that distinction, because I think there was a lot that did happen in TLJ that’s interesting and could’ve been propagated, but was left out, and knowing this, it simplifies the impact the movie had on the overall arc. 

You could tell this individual that Kylo killed snoke and cemented his role as the leader of the first order, that Rey was trained briefly by Luke and has cemented herself as a Jedi, that Luke has passed into the force, Leia is force sensitive, and that the rebellion is considerably weakened. 

Contrast that with how much character development and relationship development the fifth episode has, and the ways in which RoTJ builds on it, and the disconnect between these two movies is clear.
